attributes.body_ja:
助動詞（じょどうし）「う」または「よう」に「とする」が付（つ）くと、「(A) をするつもりだ」や「(A) をする直前（ちょくぜん）だ」という意味（いみ）を表（あらわ）します。この格助詞（かくじょし）の「と」は「結果（けっか）」を表（あらわ）します。

「ようとする」と使（つか）うときは、(A) の動詞（どうし）を「う」や「よう」の意向形（いこうけい）にして、そのあとに「とする」を付（つ）けます。

「う」と「よう」は、何（なに）かをする意思（いし）があることを表（あらわ）します。これに「とする」を加（くわ）えることで、その意思（いし）は固（かた）まっていて、あとは実際（じっさい）に行動（こうどう）するだけというようなニュアンスが出（で）ます。「(A) しようと努力（どりょく）する」というニュアンスを含（ふく）むこともあります。また、「する」が過去形（かこけい）の場合（ばあい）は、「試（ため）してみたけど、失敗（しっぱい）した」ような意味（いみ）になることが多（おお）いです。

注意点（ちゅういてん）

「ようとする」は、何（なに）かをしようと思（おも）っていたら、別（べつ）の出来事（できごと）が起（お）きる場面（ばめん）でもよく使（つか）われます。この場合（ばあい）は「努力（どりょく）する」というよりも、「(A) をする直前（ちょくぜん）に、予想（よそう）していなかった (B) が起（お）きた」のような意味（いみ）になります。
attributes.body:
When combined with the auxiliary verb う (or よう), とする carries the meaning of 'to try to do (A)', or 'to be about to do (A)'. The case marking particle と in this expression highlights a 'result'.

To use おうとする, modify the (A) verb into its う or よう receiving form, and then add とする.

As う and よう mark volition (the express intent to do something), とする adds the nuance that the express intent has been decided, and all that remains is to 'do' the action. This translates quite closely to 'to endeavor to do' in English, where the past form 'endeavored to do' will suggest that the attempt was unsuccessful.

Caution

ようとする is also regularly used to indicate when one action interrupts another. In these cases, the nuance is not quite 'to have endeavored', but more '(A) was already underway, when (B)'. Again, it will just show that the (A) action was decided upon 100%, when something caused an unexpected change.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.body: ようにする (literally, 'do things in such a way as to X') expresses taking care to perform a certain action and often indicates a habitual effort. In contrast, Verb[volitional] + とする implies a one-time attempt to do something, often implying the attempt may not succeed. For example, 毎朝走るようにしている ('I'm making a habit of running every morning.') vs. １０キロ走ろうとしたけど ('I tried to run 10k, but...' implying 'but I couldn't finish', etc.).

first_relatable.title: ようにする
first_relatable.meaning: To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to

second_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
second_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: These two expressions are opposite uses of the same structure. Verb[volitional]とする means 'Try to do (A)' or 'Make an attempt at (A)', often with the nuance that the attempt may fail, e.g. 食べようとしたけど、無理だった 'I tried to eat it, but I couldn't.' In contrast, 〜ようとしない means 'Not even try to (A)', e.g. うちの息子は、野菜を食べようとしない 'My son doesn't even try to eat vegetables.'

first_relatable.title: 〜ようとしない
first_relatable.meaning: Not willing to, Not make an effort to, To not attempt or try to, Volitional + としない

second_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
second_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: Both structures use the volitional verb form to show intent, but differ in whether the outcome is explicitly expressed. 'Verb[volitional]とする' expresses an attempt or intention to do something, e.g. '食べようとする' ('try to eat'). 'Verb[volitional]としたが' implies the attempt was interrupted or failed, e.g. '食べようとしたが、無理だった' ('I tried to eat it, but couldn't').

first_relatable.title: Verb[volitional] + としたが
first_relatable.meaning: Tried to ~ but ~, Was about to ~ but ~, Was going to ~ but ~

second_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
second_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: The grammar point 'Verb[volitional]とする' expresses the speaker's decision or intention to do something, often indicating a plan or goal. In contrast, 'まだ～ていません' is used to express that an action has not yet occurred or a state has not yet been reached, emphasizing the ongoing absence of the action or state.

first_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
first_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: Both can describe actions about to happen, but with different nuance. るところだ simply states that something is on the verge of occurring. Verb[volitional] + とする adds a sense of intent or effort, and is often used when the action may not actually happen, e.g. 子どもはなんでも食べようとする ('Kids will try to eat anything.'), where 食べるところだ wouldn't be appropriate.

first_relatable.title: るところだ
first_relatable.meaning: About to, On the verge of

second_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
second_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: Verb[volitional]とする and てみる are both translated as 'try', but the former implies attempting something that may not succeed, e.g. 話そうとした ('I tried to speak.'), which implies that maybe the attempt was unsuccessful. In contrast,てみる focuses on trying something to see the result, as in 話してみた ('I tried speaking.'), which has the nuance of doing so to see what it was like.

first_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
first_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to

attributes.body: Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with とする, it shows an attempt to do something, often one that fails, e.g. 食べようとしたけど ('I tried to eat it, but...'). The key difference is suggestion/proposal vs. attempted action.

first_relatable.title: Verb[volitional]とする
first_relatable.meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to
